newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebel Maskhadov claims victory in Chechen poll.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Maskhadov claims victory in Chechen poll.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who forced Russian troops out of Chechnya with a combination of guerrilla warfare and shrewd diplomacy, claimed a sweeping victory on Tuesday in its presidential election.

"I'm delighted the people made the right choice," Maskhadov told reporters as early data on Monday's polls credited him with more than 50 percent of the vote, enough for a clear victory that would avoid the need for a second round.
However, the Chechen electoral commission has not released any voting or turnout figures.

The commission's chairman Mumadi Saydaiyev told a news conference he and his colleagues were annoyed by unauthorised leaks of early returns and had decided not to issue any information before Wednesday when the count was finally completed.
The likely Maskhadov win will add weight to Chechen demands for independence. But Moscow still holds strong cards in its efforts to hang on to the tiny landlocked region.

Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet artillery colonel who led Chechnya's guerrilla army to a stunning victory in the two-year war, chided rebel hardliner Shamil Basayev, 32. But he promised to work with any of his former allies.
Basayev, speaking at his headquarters in the devastated capital Grozny, ruled out working in Maskhadov's government unless he made changes in his inner circle.
"I don't have any policy differences with Maskhadov. I said a long time ago that I will not be in his team unless he changes his entourage," Basayev told Reuters.
He accused Maskhadov of surrounding himself with "Soviet bureaucrats" who were "robbing the population".
Victory by Maskhadov, who had struck the latest peace deal with Russia, rather than Basayev, whom it wants for a bloody 1995 hostage raid on a Russian town, may be of some comfort to the Kremlin.
President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia, gave a cautious welcome to the likely Maskhadov win.

"The preliminary results of the voting, in the president's opinion, give a serious chance for productive negotiations to continue between the federal government and the new Chechen leadership," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters.
But he made clear Moscow still ruled out full independence for Chechnya.
Maskhadov said he was no less of a secessionist than Basayev or acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who was expected to finish third in the polls.
"We have had our independence from Russia since 1991 and all that now remains is for other countries, including Russia, to recognise that," he told a news conference.

Maskhadov said his first priority would be to give Chechnya's million or so people a chance to recover from the war, in which tens of thousands were killed and hundreds of thousands lost their homes. He promised to crack down on lawlessness.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), whose 72 observers monitored the polling, issued a report praising the elections as reflecting "the free will of those entitled to vote" and creating a "legitimate" new government.

The Kremlin, worried for its own stability and concerned about other restless ethnic minorities, has a strong hand against Chechnya, which is surrounded by Russian territory on three sides and backs the Caucasus mountains.
Moscow has threatened to sever relations with any nation that recognises Chechen sovereignty.

Despite sympathy for the suffering of Chechen civilians after Yeltsin unleashed his army against the region's self-declared independent government in 1994, the West has no interest in seeing Russia start to fall apart.

Maskhadov, whom aides said had 58 percent of the early count to 30 percent for Basayev, wants "war reparations". Russia has promised cash for rebuilding, notably Chechnya's oil refineries. Those funds will be a vital bargaining chip.
